newsitem.title: USA: FOCUS - Motorola forecast batters stock.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Motorola forecast batters stock.

text.p: Motorola Inc.'s stock was hammered Wednesday after the maker of electronic equipment and components forecast that its third-quarter earnings will be down sharply from the second quarter.
Motorola lost $1.625 to $49 on heavy trading of more than 7.4 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange, where it was the most active issue.
Motorola, which makes cellular telephones and computer equipment such as semiconductors and integrated circuits, also said its earnings would be lower than Wall Street analysts had projected.
The company said its projection of a potential "significant drop" in third-quarter earnings from the second quarter's results could mean a decline of 25 percent or more.

In a conference call, Motorola did not specify the amount of the decline. But Edward Gams, vice president and director of investor relations, said Motorola normally uses the term "significant" to describe a change of 25 percent or more.
The company earned $326 million, or 54 cents a share, on sales of $6.83 billion in the second quarter.
According to First Call, which tracks analysts' earnings estimates, Motorola had been expected to earn 50 cents a share in the current quarter.
Noting that the semiconductor industry remained in a "down cycle," Motorola said the most significant factor affecting the results was poor demand and low prices in its semicondoctor division.

However, other chip makers posted gains Wednesday, a day after the the Semiconductor Industry Association said in its monthly report that the ratio of new orders to shipments of computer chips was at 0.90 in August, up from 0.86 a month earlier.
But analysts said Motorola's cellular phone, paging and modem businesses might be more troubling than semiconductors.
Motorola said price pressure persisted on its cellular phone, paging and modem businesses, and in international markets, orders and sales have weakened.
Cellular competition will pressure prices long-term, while Motorola's semiconductor business will likely turn around with the industry in the medium term, analysts said.

"The cellular handset pricing competition continues to be strong and ferocious as analog spills over into digital," said Rakesh Sood, an analyst for Hambrecht & Quist. "Our expectation is (the competition) will continue for some time."

Motorola's general systems sector (which includes cellular phones and pagers) made up about 40 percent of total revenues in the last quarter, while semiconductors accounted for about 29 percent, analysts said.

Gary Tooker, vice chairman and chief executive officer, said many of Motorola's units have taken steps to reduce expenses, including hiring restrictions and reductions in work schedules and manufacturing run rates. They also have reduced capital expenditures, especially in the semiconductor products sector.
The company is expected to report its third-quarter results on Oct. 7.
Analysts agreed Motorola may cut operating costs further, and one said it may even have to restructure. In July Motorola was forced to lay off employees for the first time in more than a decade.
"I'm virtually convinced there will actually be people laid off," said Scott Wright, an analyst for Argus Research, who has followed the company for about two years.
"I wouldn't be surprised to hear more specific news on the restructuring front," he said.
Tough times could also be with Motorola shareholders for some time, said analysts.

"I would think Motorola may be dead money for a while," said Robert Stovall, president of Stovall/21st Advisors. "It won't rally for the next few weeks since the third-quarter comments repeated the second-quarter profit margin problems."
Stovall said investors could also sell Motorola shares to recognize losses for tax purposes late this year, which would only prolong the malaise.
